endorsements.quote: Monitoring needs a named owner: in practice, a designated clinical lead for each deployed tool, supported by an embedded analytics or quality-and-safety unit reporting to an existing clinical governance committee, rather than a new parallel structure.

Hence, the implementation of AI occurs in an LHS is an iterative concrete learning cycle: silent evaluation of candidate tools against local data before go-live; staged deployment against pre-specified performance and equity thresholds; dashboards surveilling accuracy, calibration and subgroup bias in routine operations; and scheduled recalibration or retirement decisions taken by governance committees.
routine subgroup monitoring of accuracy and bias so inequitable performance is detected rather than assumed away.

Bias surveillance and recalibration can be resourced proportionately through automated dashboards and periodic sampling-based audits rather than continuous manual review, and through procurement contracts that assign vendors explicit performance-maintenance obligations.

AI differs from many prior healthcare innovations in that its performance is dynamic, shifting with data, workflows and population, thereby requiring continuous, rather than episodic, evaluation and adaptation.

Hence, the implementation of AI occurs in an LHS is an iterative concrete learning cycle: silent evaluation of candidate tools against local data before go-live; staged deployment against pre-specified performance and equity thresholds; dashboards surveilling accuracy, calibration and subgroup bias in routine operations; and scheduled recalibration or retirement decisions taken by governance committees.

unlisted_practices: Embed AI implementation within a Learning Health System with permanent operational infrastructure so monitoring continues after project funding ends.
Use CFIR to assess organizational readiness, context, workflow fit, governance and equity before AI implementation.
Co-produce AI tools with patients, clinicians, data scientists and managers, including underserved communities, rather than tokenistic consultation.
Integrate AI oversight into existing quality-and-safety infrastructure rather than creating a parallel structure.
Resource-constrained systems should adopt few high-value AI tools, sequence adoption against LHS maturity, and pool monitoring capacity through regional or network-level shared services.
Use shared or federated infrastructure and validation and transparent benchmarking to lower entry costs and make adoption and performance gaps visible across sites.
Use implementation strategy compilations such as ERIC to select strategies matched to identified determinants.

screen.reason: This is a commentary arguing for the use of Learning Health System (LHS) and implementation science frameworks to govern, deploy, and continuously monitor AI responsibly in healthcare.
